en: *The Essential Art of Embodying Benevolence*, one scroll.
Preface to the Wenxing Pavilion’s Reorganized Society for the Release of Living Creatures by Peng Shaosheng.
The Wenxing Pavilion’s Society for the Release of Living Creatures was initiated by my late great-great-grandfather, Lord Nanjun, and has continued until the present day for several decades.
Many years passed. In the thirty-ninth year of the Qianlong era, he first established a *fangsheng chi* (refuge pond for living beings) at the Mulberry-Plum Bridge in the Southern Garden;
here, the keeping of fish became particularly flourishing. Furthermore, he set aside a portion of the vacant space within the pavilion to raise sheep, pigs, chickens, and ducks.
Once these were full, they were sent to Yunqi. In recent four or five years, the annual expenditure on feed has reached sixty or seventy taels of silver.

Yet those attending the assembly were so few as to number no more than a handful; even exhausting all available resources, it was still insufficient, meaning that fish and birds who might have benefited from its bounty were but few.
I now propose to reorganize this former assembly, appointing twelve stewards for each month.
A person maintains a ledger. Each year, they recruit people to contribute three hundred and sixty coins; ten such contributions yield three thousand six hundred coins, which constitute one share.
Twelve shares accumulated result in forty thousand coins and more. With these funds, they purchase living creatures for release at appropriate times.
If there is a surplus, it is used to provide food supplies; if there is a deficiency, they recruit others to provide replacements. In this manner, the practice gradually increases by multiples.
The number is incalculable. Households with fields may contribute a portion of their provisions, which can be commuted for money.

Every year on the third day of the second month, they collectively offer prayers at the Guixiang Hall; when winter ends, they engage monks to recite sutras, dedicating the merit toward rebirth in the Western Pure Land.
This shall cause both the donor and the recipient to create the causes for long life and plant the seeds of the fruit of Bodhi.

If one can devote oneself to this practice with diligence and without slackening for the duration of one's entire life, the resulting merit will be inconceivable. However, I fear that you, honorable sirs, may only occasionally give rise to a virtuous mind.

They soon regress and fall back. Upon examining their origins, it is evident they are not without obscurations and hindrances. To summarize the general outline, I have categorized them into eight points.
Do not dismiss this as mere pedantry; I hope you will deign to consider it.

Some may say that the five constant virtues constitute the nature, while the Way encompasses all myriad goodnesses. Yet, how could this mere act of moistening one another with saliva compare to the measure of vast magnanimity?
They fail to realize that among the virtues of the five constants, benevolence (*ren*) is foremost; and among the gates to the myriad goodnesses, love (*ai*) is the most expansive.

Sacrificing a single ox can surely ensure the security of the people; releasing a single fawn can provide a fruit worthy of entrusting the state. To love one’s own life and extend that love to the lives of others—this is the "square rule" (jueju).
To cease one’s own killing so as to save others from being killed—this is called "extending grace. A single basketful of earth eventually completes a mountain;
how difficult is it for a drop of water to reach the sea?

Some might say that one’s own kin and the people differ in their degree of intimacy, as do the people and other creatures; since these distinctions exist, one ought to differentiate between what is urgent and what is not.

Yet they fail to realize that no calamity is more惨烈 (cānlè) than perilous ruin, and no act of compassion precedes the saving of a quivering, trembling creature. Consider the common folk who till the soil and dig for roots—they have long been spared from the fires of cauldrons.
Since time immemorial, during the kalpa of warfare, what has been more惨烈 (cānlè) than the slaughterhouse? One cannot help but be struck with alarm at the sight of a parched carriage track.
To begrudge a single cup of water while greedily gulping at a butcher’s gate—who has ever heard such a sound in the dead of night?
Some may say that Heaven created birds and beasts solely to nourish humans; yet these creatures are but dull and insentient things—what benefit is there in releasing them?

One must realize that Heaven covers all universally, viewing humans and animals as one and the same. All beings crave life; self and other are of a single essence. If one were to say that [one eats] meat...

To nourish others, it is not appropriate to further increase the cultivation of vegetables and grains. If you intend to honor humans and debase livestock, how can you compare yourself to jackals and wolves?

If your benevolent arts are not yet sufficient, you are merely a discarded object between heaven and earth. Do not fail to hold yourself accountable, and do not recklessly pry into the mysteries of Heaven.

Some may say that the *I Ching* prizes the grand feast and the *Book of Rites* honors the special slaughter of animals; since fishing and hunting were not abolished, how could fish and birds be deemed objects of pity?
Yet they fail to realize that when music was performed for the nine rounds at the court of Shun, there was the auspicious omen of all creatures dancing in harmony;

and when King Tang opened the nets on three sides, the *Book of Shang* records the text of universal compliance. It was only because their capacity for compassion was so expansive as to leave nothing behind that their grace flowed beyond all bounds. This is why...

To bestow life is to necessarily cherish it; this remains the spirit of the "Sparse Waters" (Shuishu). To observe the pheasant with reverence is a heart that reaches far beyond the composition at the mountain beam.
If the mechanism for killing has not yet been exhausted, how can one’s great virtue be fully realized?
Some may say: "Within a single region, in the course of a single day, those killed are exceedingly many while those released are exceedingly few.

Judging by this standard against that, how could they possibly save one another? They do not realize that in a year of great drought, the water from a single irrigation channel can still sustain several mu of fields;
and on a day of bitter cold, a single fur cloak can still revive the life of one person. It begins with...

To protect life by means of killing; to continue the cycle of killing in order to preserve life. Provided that one’s power of aspiration remains firm and steadfast, all demons will surely be repelled and dispersed.
Some may argue:

"If one habitually eats meat and only releases living beings on this single day, it is like one day of heat followed by ten days of cold; what benefit does this bring to the cause? Such people do not understand.
The right hand strikes a person, while the left hand supports them; the kindness of the one who supports may somewhat offset the cruelty of the one who strikes.
To slander the Buddha for a thousand days and then to recite his name for a single day—the sin of the slanderer may still be extinguished by the sincerity of the one who recites his name.
The vigorous emergence of the vital impulse is precisely the manifestation of the Heavenly Principle. One must simply discard the old to plan for the new;
how could one possibly follow the current without turning back?
Some might say: "Having just escaped from the cage, one is stalked by hunters in the forest; having just parted from the net, bait is dangled at the shore.
With no way to advance or retreat, even with compassion, how could one be saved? Yet they do not realize that a prisoner facing execution merely wishes for a brief reprieve from death.
Such a gift of renewed life would already be a grace encompassing the vastness of heaven and earth. As for the killer, let them kill.
Fixed karma is difficult to escape; that which arises does so of its own accord. Strive, therefore, to exhaustively fulfill this mind.
Some may say that the sprouting of compassion arises merely from a sudden encounter, and that once birth and extinction are exhausted, one accords with True Suchness (*tathatā*).

How can one allow for the seeking [of truth] through attachment to forms? How could such a person recognize the Way of Non-action (*wuwei*)? They do not know that the mind of a sudden encounter is, by its very nature, eternally abiding.

Because it is eternally abiding, True Suchness (Tathatā) does not become obscured by not perceiving external objects; yet, because it does not abandon the conditioned (saṃskṛta), it does not fall into the attachment to a biased emptiness.
If one were to definitively interpret it as being unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), how would that differ from the folly of clinging to signs?
This is the refuge of those who resort to false evasions; one must certainly eliminate such views and remain free from delusion.
Petition for the Establishment of a *Fangsheng* (Releasing Living Creatures) Assembly at Wenshengge Pavilion, by Xue Qifeng.

I humbly submit that Heaven and Earth establish their positions; "Great Virtue" is called life. The Sage accomplishes his capacity; his divine prowess does not kill. The Three Powers stand in mutual relation;
man alone possesses the harmony of the vital breath (*chongqi*). The Four Virtues are practiced in tandem; "Origin" (*yuan*) is the very basis of sustaining life. Pushing back the flow of qi...

At the very beginning of form, the hundred clans shared a single source. Examining the profound transformation within the flowing currents, all things coexist without mutual harm. Floating and sinking, ascending and descending, they blend together to transform into a refined essence.
Among all sentient beings, there are none that do not cherish their lives; as long as one belongs to the realm of the emotional and conscious, all know the love for their own existence.
Looking back to the Great Antiquity, the world was simple and the people were pure; humans and creatures forgot each other’s presence, and creatures and humans [forgot each other's presence].

They governed together. The animals shed their coats and bred their young; they were recorded only in the annals of spring and autumn. Amidst rain and wind, birds flew and beasts ran, yet none were harmed or startled.

One could look down upon bird nests without fear, and swimming fish remained undisturbed. Thus, the qilin and phoenix appeared in the outskirts, while tortoises and dragons were tame in the ponds. Among the people, there were no premature deaths or pestilence.
Things were not yet subject to violent disorder before the five cycles of the Dao’s radiance; spring reigned during the era of the Three Sovereigns.

This is what is meant by "each rectifying its nature and destiny" and "preserving and harmonizing the Great Harmony," acting without conscious striving or knowing in accordance with the patterns of the Emperor (Heaven).

It was for this reason that Confucius sighed over the Great Unity (*Datong*), and why the Master of Old (*Laozi*) was able to know the primordial beginning. Since the human mind has been daily excavated, the Great Simplicity has gradually...
As carvings [of beasts] proliferated, lustful thoughts surged upward; as various vapors circulated, they began to consume fur and drink blood, all while harboring a competitive spirit.

Eating meat and wearing silk eventually became habitual customs. Nets, snares, arrows, and spears covered the hills and filled the depths; fresh fish and dried meats were butchered and cooked to fill the kitchens and adorn the sacrificial tables.
Used daily without reflection, these acts were treated as if they were natural. Although the Supreme Deity loves all living beings, He could not save them from this state.
When objects fall beneath the blade, living beings beg for their lives; yet they have no means to appeal to Heaven while within the cauldrons and boiling pots.

From this mechanism of killing, the cycles of kalpas are consequently brought to fruition. The calamities of water, fire, and weapons arise, and the afflictions of drought, floods, disease, and pestilence emerge.
This principle does not come from without; it is fundamentally brought about by oneself. The Sage, following human sentiments, established regulations for them. Not...
Having obtained this, one eliminates extravagance. The six departments—the soil and the grain—are well-cultivated; the nine gates are secured so that no birds escape from the nets and snares.

Hearing the cry of an animal or seeing it being slaughtered, one realizes that benevolence is far from the kitchen. With plain wine and unseasoned broth, the true flavor is preserved even in the great feasts. Thus, the subtle application of ritual and instruction is achieved.

It implicitly embodies compassion. Since the teachings were propagated from the Western Regions and their transformation spread to the Eastern Land, the flowing water has rescued the parched, and the name of the Precious Victorious One has been invoked.
During the Putong era, the text on abstaining from meat was proclaimed; in the Dali era, the stone for releasing living beings was inscribed. Thus, all myriad species are nurtured with warmth.

They rescue and deliver beings from the three miserable realms. Other instances include dredging ponds to nurture fish, casting away bows to spare deer, releasing turtles to save ants, and setting free carp to revive birds;
these deeds are recorded in the annals and all manifest the response of merit. How much more so when one reverently examines past precedents and exhaustively probes the workings of the Creator!
The wild goose is also called the King; the deer can give birth to daughters; the son of the White Emperor becomes a snake; the messenger of the Queen Mother becomes a magpie;
the youth in green robes leaves medicinal formulas among mankind; and the man of embroidered capes stirs wind and thunder upon the river.

This is where the mechanism of transformation operates in secret, its profound resonance difficult to perceive. To know the subtle and the manifest—to possess such spiritual and sagely power—is something that cannot be fully detailed through thought or deliberation;
it is beyond what can be reached by ordinary consciousness or intellectual understanding. I reverently reflect upon His Majesty, the Emperor Yuan:
he nurtures goodness and embodies the primal source, securing eternal life for the people. By perfecting human nature, he perfects the nature of all things; the Way resides within him.

With utmost sincerity, you skillfully save all things and skillfully save all people; your merit accords with the Great Creator. We disciples vow in our hearts to repent of our sins and resolve to repay your kindness.

Having fortunately been sustained by your life-giving grace and having received your instructions and admonitions, we desire to reach the path of the Celestial Nature. First, we rely upon the gateway of merit and virtue.
We have observed that the people of Suzhou are numerous and flourishing, yet their customs are extravagant and indulgent; they dwell by the water and produce goods from the land.
Valleys are choked and rivers overflow; fishing households and butcher shops line the streets and stand in rows at the markets.

The lives of sentient beings are maimed and destroyed, their number exceeding the sands of the Ganges, as they indulge in nourishing their physical forms in vain, filling the celestial moats to no purpose.

Fearing that their karmic retribution will cause them to sink into an endless cycle of rebirths, and being unable to transform the great earth into a lush forest or the vast ocean into a sacred preserve, one must inevitably rely upon the ground of goodness to welcome and guide the rebirth of the spirit.

The Sage, in his proximity, promotes the benevolence of a single thought and skillfully preserves the lives of all sentient beings. At Wensheng Pavilion, there was formerly a society for releasing living creatures;

now, I pray that we shall together relinquish pure wealth to continue cultivating virtuous deeds. May each person rely upon the power of their vows, and according to what they see and hear, fulfill the source of compassion.
By extending the feeling of "not being able to bear" [the suffering of others] to all that can be endured, one accords with the nature of purity and tranquility, mindful of our own lives.

May it not differ from the birth of others. We hope that virtuous influences will permeate and ascend, so that auspiciousness may arrive and abide, the three calamities shall not arise, and the eight difficulties shall silently vanish.
May yin and yang harmonize so that wind and rain come in their proper seasons; may things flourish and be perfected so that the people are healthy and long-lived.

Therefore, we venture to purify ourselves and face the divine, expressing our words with fervent urgency. We humbly pray that Your Majesty, the Primordial August Emperor, will bestow the power of compassion and forbearance, opening the gate of sweetness...
Opening the gate of the Dharma, I take pity on those who are deluded and seek to open their eyes to pure faith.

My endeavor is to cause every person to give rise to compassion based on the realization of our shared essence, and further to hope that in every generation they shall form societies for the release of living beings. From the closest kin to all others, may they equally roam in the vast and boundless heavens;

through love, may they perfect benevolence, and together enjoy the joy of peace and tranquility. This is indeed the seed of merit for the ten stages of the bodhisattva path, and truly the provision for the myriad virtues.
I hope that these may be fulfilled and that we may yet find mutual accord. Overwhelmed by the utmost trepidation and awe, I respectfully submit this memorial for your consideration.
Dedication Text for the Release of Living Beings, by Peng Shaosheng.

I, the disciple Shao-sheng, vow that all sentient beings may be delivered and be reborn together in the Pure Land. Therefore, at the Wensheng Pavilion in this county, I have convened a ceremony for the release of living beings.
For the sake of all present sentient beings, we take refuge in the Triple Gem and chant the names of the Buddhas.
May all sentient beings, relying upon the Buddha’s compassion, be equally received into his protection. From this day forth until the end of the future, may they sever...

May all terrors be exhausted and all afflictions eradicated. May they no longer devour, bite, contend with, or kill one another, but instead advance in the practice of the Buddha-dharma and escape the sea of suffering.
Furthermore, for the sake of the assembled disciples, I shall repent for and eliminate the various karmic conditions of killing and eating meat accumulated since beginningless time.
I pray that the sentient beings who were killed and those whose flesh was eaten may rely upon the Buddha’s compassion.

May they all be compassionately gathered and transformed; may their hearts of enmity and poison be converted so that they face one another with joy, attain rebirth in the good realms, and together bathe in the great waves of grace.

We, the disciples, pray that once we have been born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī), we shall return to this Sahā world to universally transform sentient beings, forever severing the causes of killing and abiding in inexhaustible life.
We dedicate these roots of goodness toward non-retrogressive Bodhi. We respectfully beseech the Tathāgata to bear witness.
May you know my vow; it is true and not false. May all beings within the three realms of existence and the four debts of gratitude together perfect the seed of omniscience.
The Stele for the Pond for Releasing Living Creatures at Nanyuan, Peng Shaosheng, Suzhou.
Anciently, this was a marshland state. The waters surrounding the prefecture consist of rivers and lakes as their largest features, while those that are smaller are...
The rivers, harbors, and streams are so numerous as to be beyond counting. All the sentient beings dwelling in the waters, whether large or small, have flourished and multiplied therein;
indeed, there should be nothing that cannot find refuge within them. Yet, those who exploit them increase day by day, while those who govern them grow ever more constrained.
Looking around at this state of affairs, it is difficult to find even a single scale or a solitary creature that dwells in peace and enjoys its life. How difficult!
How tragic! Thereupon, the worthy ones of our school gave rise to a heart of compassion and, following the conduct of a Bodhisattva, established a monthly assembly for the release of living beings.
They subsequently converted the garden into a pond to provide them with a secure dwelling and invited monks to guard it.

Taking as their precedent the story of the Elder Flowing Water who saved the fish, they named the site "The Flowing Water Chan Hermitage," so that all sentient beings might forever sever the habit of killing.

Thus, the innate nature of all beings is fulfilled; they do not remain confined to their respective quarters, but like a vast expanse of water, they bathe in the sun and moon, surging with waves and leaping through the clouds, rejoicing in our Great Peace and perpetuating their descendants for eternity.
How magnificent is the Way of the Sage! How radiant is the Wind of the King! Beholding this, one cannot help but dance with hands and leap with feet. This is to know where one returns.
The student, meeting with these supreme conditions, joined his palms in praise and inscribed this eulogy:
Heaven gave birth to the myriad tribes, And once their dwellings were established, Birds have the mountains and forests, Fish have the rivers and lakes.
Each maintains its own boundaries, None encroach upon one another; Preserving the Great Harmony, They reach equality with Heaven.
Humans are the most spiritual of beings; why do you not reflect upon this? The weak are devoured by the strong—how can you distinguish right from wrong?
Contemplate the original source: what person is there, and what thing? Let the world be at ease within its natural freedom, where purity and tranquility are unified.
Bound by habitual tendencies, the karma of killing blazes forth: arrows leave no forest untouched, and nets leave no river unsearched.
Alas, you people! Who among you does not loathe death? When thorns and brambles pierce the body, the cries of pain never cease.
Yet you indulge your mouths and bellies, boiling the fat and striking down the fresh; wherever the blade and the block pass, the calamity of blackened death fills the heavens.
Do not say that these are but fish, for though their forms are minute, they possess the nature of living beings and share the same vital breath as Heaven and Earth.
When you eat this fish, you wound the root of Heaven and Earth; yet you do not realize it, for your mind is clouded.
You have a wife and family, and the fish has its own mate; they moisten and nourish one another until death.
When the knife is applied and slaughter occurs, whether sooner or later makes no difference. If you do not love the fish, why do you not love yourself?
Alas for you, O people! You are muddled through the three periods of existence. If one observes with the eye of wisdom, all is one and non-dual.
Prince Liu-li, in a former life, was a fisherman. The fish he caught became a king; he killed men as he had killed fish—this is what karma accomplishes.
It turns like a waterwheel; danger changes as quickly as walking upon hoarfrost. This is because one did not discern it early on.
The Buddha speaks and Confucius speaks; with different mouths but one voice, the Great Virtuous One says "life.
The mind of Confucius and the mind of the Buddha both seek to save the life of things. They prohibit your killing, using life to stop killing—this is the Dharma of remediation.
There is no self and no objects; when life arises, it is non-arising. Whether it be the birth of the self or the birth of objects, all return together to the City of Enlightenment.
The Stele for the Peng Family’s Pond for Releasing Living Creatures, by Peng Shaosheng, Qianlong 17th Year.

When my late father served as the Provincial Education Commissioner in Zhejiang, he visited his home village and ordered his sons, including Peng Shaoqian, to designate a vacant plot behind the residence as a garden.
Taking advantage of the low-lying terrain, they constructed a pond; the pond is approximately half a *mu* in area and was planted with—

I kept a few carp and crucian fish. Several years later, while Shao-sheng was reading in the garden, he would occasionally purchase fish from the market and release them into the pond, taking pleasure in watching them swim and play.

After more than twenty years had passed, the fish in the pond became exceedingly numerous; indeed, among my family members and descendants, those who were born and raised during these twenty-odd years [numbered many].
There are perhaps no fewer than thirty such people who receive the bounty of Heaven and Earth and are bathed in the transformation of the Great Peace.
As I give life to all living things, they are neither "this" nor "that"; drawn forward by the sun and grown by the moon, they flourish together without harm.
Thus, I have requested permission from my late father to erect a stele by the pond, inscribed with the title "Pond for Receiving Life. I hereby compose this inscription to show it to my descendants.
The Inscription reads: The fish in the pond are numerous; The Peng clan is vast. The fish in the pond are abundant; The Peng clan is continuous.
This is the essential art of embodying benevolence. (End)
